prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled clocks of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock as a sole prize part and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Having read the full exchange, the scientific case has not weakened under questioning. The magic-wavelength lattice removes the trapping Stark shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement suppresses Doppler and recoil effects, so many neutral atoms can be interrogated at once on a narrow optical transition. That is a distinct invention and not a refinement of an existing method, and it brought systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18. The interpretation is not in question: independent laboratories reproduce, compare and surpass the early results, and use the clocks for redshift measurements at millimetre scale, limits on varying constants and the preparation of a new definition of the second. I also reasoned about it as a discovery-first case, as the committee should. The identifiable people are a pair with complementary contributions, Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking the system to record accuracy and coherence, and no member has proposed a different or third name. In answer to the chair's question on the 2005 and 2012 prizes, I consider the distinction sufficient if the citation names the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, because the comb is a readout tool and ion control is a different physical regime. I would keep the redefinition of the second out of the citation, since it follows from the work and is not the reason to honour it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that a sceptic can read the lattice clock as an extraordinary but incremental step in a metrology lineage already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and that the committee then awards a third precision-measurement prize. The credit is also not perfectly clean: Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and ion-clock pioneers are outside the two names, and the split between Katori's concept and Ye's performance work is partly intertwined historically. I am recalling priority from general knowledge and have not verified the dates of the first proposal against the first demonstrations from documents in the files, so the committee should treat that point as unconfirmed. Finally, if the committee wishes to hold metrology prizes until the SI redefinition is concluded, that is a timing argument that I find weak but cannot exclude. Against B007 specifically, I weigh the conceptual importance of topological insulators as higher than that of the clock, which is why it remains my alternative, but the credit problem there is a structural defect and not a long tail.

responses.point: Olsson prefers topological insulators (B007) as a sole part, citing the new organising principle of a Z2 invariant, the clean theory-to-measurement chain through the HgTe conductance result, and its top-four ranking by all eight members, while conceding that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap cannot be repaired within three names.
responses.response: I agree that B007 is the more fundamental idea and I do not dismiss it, as the breadth of support for it is real. But your own case against decides the matter for me. If the BHZ proposal was indispensable to the HgTe observation, which you say the committee cannot rule out, then the three names cannot be fair, and Zhang's death means no wording can repair it. For B056 the omissions are later implementers and parallel groups, and both originators are alive and named. I also still weigh the 2016 prize against B007 somewhat: the Z2 step is new, but Kane-Mele sits on a conceptual line that was recognised. Being the only candidate every member ranked is a consensus fact about stature and not about the credit question we must settle, so I do not treat it as a substitute for judgment.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the Kane-Mele Z2 classification changed how band structures are analysed, including routine first-principles computation of Z2 invariants, and treats the BHZ omission as regrettable but not disqualifying because the concept and invariant belong to Kane and Mele.
responses.response: The routine use of Z2 invariants in materials work is a strong argument for the impact of the concept, and I accept it. The weak point is the step from concept to prize: the experimental leg of your trio rests on a platform that someone else proposed, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan is close enough to the same idea that a citation would be contested on both sides. You could answer the chair's question by wording the citation around the invariant and the helical edge state, and I would then move B007 higher, but I do not think wording removes the fact that the person who identified HgTe is not among the laureates. I would rather see the committee return to B007 with a documented account of who proposed what than decide this year on recollection.

responses.point: Johansson supports B056 but adds B037, Hosono's iron-based high-temperature superconductors, as a second part, on the grounds that both have unambiguous attribution and that the open pairing mechanism is an interpretation gap and not a gap in the discovery. Johansson concedes that the two parts have almost nothing in common and that Hosono has thin support.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between discovery and mechanism, and I am consistent on this: I do not treat an unsettled pairing mechanism as disqualifying in itself. But the reasoning that supports B037 does not carry the second part. The discovery is well replicated, yet the rapid multi-group follow-up by Chinese, Japanese and other groups means that a sole-laureate share is exactly the credit imbalance you identify yourself, and I ranked B037 seventh. A second part that the proposer himself describes as unrelated and thinly supported is an argument for using the three-name allowance, not a reason to use it. Since B056 is already complete with two names, I see no scientific gain in adding a part, and I would not pair the two in order to fit a limit.

responses.point: Kroll holds that for the lattice clock the discovery, attribution and maturity all point the same way, with Katori conceiving and first demonstrating the clock and Ye taking it to extreme accuracy, while openly admitting that priority for the concept cannot be fully separated from priority for the performance demonstrations.
responses.response: I share this reading, and I want to be explicit about the one point where we are both exposed: neither of us has documented the priority sequence, and the chair has asked for exactly that. My answer is that the two-name credit survives either ordering, because even if a competing group had a first demonstration, the combination of the magic-wavelength concept and the development of the strontium clock to record performance is what the citation names. Your note about your time in Hall's laboratory is, in my view, a disclosure and not a recusal trigger, since it concerns the 2005 comb background and not Katori or Ye. I would not object to your participating fully.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports B056 and asks whether the SI redefinition should count as evidence of maturity, be treated as coincident or be a reason to wait, while noting the risk of weighting a metrology prize by a pending redefinition and not by a discovery about nature.
responses.response: I agree with your caution and answer the chair's question directly: the redefinition is a consequence of the physics and should not be in the citation, and it should not be a reason to wait either, since the maturity is already shown by independent laboratories agreeing near 1e-18 and by the use of the clocks for tests of constants and redshift. Lindroth and Kroll record that metrology prizes may be held back until a redefinition concludes, but that is a procedural habit and not something the scientific record supports. Where I would add to your support is on IceCube: I accept your point that neutrino astronomy is a result the committee should reward, but the attribution burden of two names for a collaboration that built on AMANDA and DUMAND is heavier than for B056, so my position on B003 stays that it belongs to a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock is judged sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether naming the magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms in the citation is enough.

Whether the priority sequence between Katori's magic-wavelength concept and the first demonstrations, and the contributions of Ludlow, Lemonde, Oates and others, would hold up under documented checking; I am recalling this from general knowledge.
Whether the committee would hold a metrology prize until the SI redefinition of the second is formally concluded.
Whether B007 could be made fair by citation wording given the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and Zhang's death, and how much the 2016 prize reduces its priority.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B012), which I opened with as first choice, is already mature enough once the pairing mechanism and the credit among early experimental groups are better understood.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections (PhD supervisor David Gross, mentor Hector Rubinstein, co-author Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group) do not coincide with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I note the disclosures by Johansson on B058 and by Kroll on the Hall laboratory and see no reason for recusal on B056 in either case; my own disclosure is unchanged from round 1.
